rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch inside the supplied facts and turns the regulatory split into a real beat story: "Whoop ships an FDA-cleared ECG and a blood-pressure feature that is deliberately not a medical device." B has useful bones, but "Whoop Finally Has FDA-Cleared ECG. Apple Watch Has Had It for Years." walks straight into an unsupplied named-competitor claim. That is not color; it is a fact-check trap in headline clothing.
gaps_in_A: "blood pressure — a feature nobody has cleared" overstates what the update gives. The facts say competitors already ship FDA-cleared ECG; they do not say nobody has cleared blood pressure.
"not the base band" is sloppy. The update says the features are gated behind the most expensive membership tier, not that a base band exists or lacks them.
"company whose entire model is subscription rather than hardware margin" leans on outside knowledge. Plausible, but not supplied; keep it as a question unless verified.
gaps_in_B: "Apple Watch Has Had It for Years" names a competitor and timeline the update did not provide. The supplied fact is generic: competitors already ship FDA-cleared ECG.
"Apple Watch includes ECG with hardware, no subscription gate — confirm this" is useful research homework, but the angle already depends on it before confirming it. Bad order.
"That's a Health Equity Story" is overclaimed. A premium paywall creates an access question; health equity needs evidence about who is excluded and why.
"The wearable industry has spent years positioning cuffless blood pressure monitoring as the next frontier" is a broad market-history claim not in the update. Either source it or cut it.
